title: Data
text:
When the quantity of interest is unobserved, I build the data. Every paper ships with a journal-grade replication archive; the datasets below are released, or built for release, as standalone public resources.
Malaysia Election Panel Data, 1959–2018. A constituency-level panel covering every Malaysian general election, built from primary electoral records with boundary harmonization across successive redistricting exercises. Available at Zenodo.
Lower Chamber Elections Archive, Malaysia. Contributed to the Constituency-Level Elections Archive (CLEA), including candidate-, district-, and party-coding corrections fed back to the archive.
Three-Country Candidate Career Panels. Career-trajectory panels for every dominant-party candidate in three regimes: the United Malays National Organisation (UMNO) in Malaysia (1959–2022), the Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) in Japan (1947–2014), and the Kuomintang (KMT) in Taiwan (1986–2024), assembled from primary records in three languages with documented codebooks. Public release planned alongside the associated paper, “Dancing with Hands Tied.”
Geocoded Settlement Layers for Peninsular Malaysia. Geocoded layers of Emergency-era Chinese New Villages and Federal Land Development Authority (FELDA) schemes, joined to historical constituency boundaries for every delineation since 1955, with census-interpolated ethnic composition. Released through the replication archives of the associated papers.

title: Research
text:
“Myth and Measurement: Spatial Heterogeneity, Ecological Fallacy, and the Urban Narrative in Peninsular Malaysia’s Electoral Politics.” 2026. Journal of East Asian Studies 26(1): 87–112. [Open Access] [Replication]
Does Malaysia vote along urban–rural lines or along ethnic ones? Combining aggregate election returns from Peninsular Malaysia with survey evidence and modeling spatial heterogeneity to guard against ecological fallacy, the paper shows that the celebrated urban–rural divide is largely an artifact of aggregation: ethnicity, not urbanization, remains the dominant cleavage structuring party competition. The result demonstrates that aggregate election data, analyzed with attention to spatial heterogeneity, can substitute for surveys in settings where reliable polling is scarce.
“Social Transformation in Malaysia and the Fragmentation of the Malay-Dominant Political Parties: Based on a Social Cleavage Structure Theory Perspective” (with Congcong Fu). Southeast Asian Studies (东南亚研究) 2021(3): 1–29. In Chinese. [Chinese Full Text] [English Translation on SSRN]
After Malaysia’s 2018 general election, five Malay-dominant parties held federal seats from Peninsular Malaysia alone, all tracing back to successive splits from UMNO. Drawing on social cleavage structure theory, the article argues that the fragmentation of Malay-dominant parties is the joint product of elite contradictions within political society and shifting cleavage structures within civil society. When intra-elite conflicts cannot be reconciled, or when a new social cleavage emerges, a new party is born; its survival depends on whether it can anchor itself to an existing or newly formed cleavage.
“Social Transformation, Dispute over Routes and the Split of Malaysian Islamic Party (PAS)” (with Congcong Fu). Southeast Asian Affairs (南洋问题研究) 2020(1): 79–95. In Chinese. [Chinese Full Text] [English Translation on SSRN]
The expansion of the Malay ethnic middle class and the imbalance of regional development weakened the Ulama faction and differentiated the professional group within the Malaysian Islamic Party (PAS), triggering a dispute over how to realize an Islamic state. The internal struggle culminated in the 2015 split that produced the National Trust Party (AMANAH). The article traces this process through the changing factional composition of PAS and argues that AMANAH’s long-term survival requires differentiated positioning relative to other Malay-based parties and a unified ideological foundation.

title: Research
text:
Under Review
“The Front Page and the Back Room: Demand Narrowing, Elite Coordination, and the Survival of Authoritarian Elites.” Under review at American Political Science Review.
When an authoritarian leader faces a crisis they may not survive, how does a divided elite coordinate on abandoning them before the moment passes? The paper argues that two features of the crisis resolve the elite’s coordination problem: a public signal that narrows the opposition’s demand onto the leader by name, making their removal a survivable exit, and a communication environment open enough for divided elites to read that narrowing as common knowledge. Where both hold, the elite sheds the leader and keeps its places; where the demand stays systemic, or never settles on a target, the elite closes ranks and the leader endures. A global-game model carries the mechanism, tested at two scales: a day-by-day reconstruction of the week of Soeharto’s fall in May 1998, coded daily across twenty-seven elites in two dailies, and a seven-crisis comparison that separates leader-removal from elite survival on the same two features. The leader falls; the elite survives.
“The Ramification of (Not) Being Governed: Colonial Rule, Social Density, and the Organization of Ethnic Politics in Post-Colonial Malaysia and Indonesia.” Under review at International Organization.
Research on colonial governance often argues that colonial states shaped post-colonial ethnic politics, but gives insufficient attention to ethnic groups’ own agency. Extending research on colonial legacies, I add a group-side variable, the baseline social density of an ethnic institution, and model its interaction with the colonial state’s decision to govern that institution or pass it over. I argue that the type of ethnic institutions that emerge, and how they interact with post-colonial states, depend on the interaction between how actively colonial states managed particular aspects of ethnic groups and how densely organized those groups were, which shaped how capable they were of resisting state intervention. Using controlled comparison and process tracing, I examine five ethnic institutions in Malaysia and Indonesia. I find that colonial-era interactions between state management and group organization can have enduring effects on post-colonial ethnic politics, even amid major political change.
“Why the Campaign Came Back: Bureaucratization and the Return of Mobilizational Governance in China.” Reject and invitation for resubmission at American Journal of Sociology.

title: Research
text:
Working Papers
“Dancing with Hands Tied: Elite Defection, Social Constraints, and the Breakdown of Dominant-Party Systems.” [SSRN]
The second paper of my dissertation, “Moving Ground.”
When and how do dominant-party systems break? The splits that end dominance begin within, after years of routine electoral dominance, led not by marginal politicians but by elites who rose nearly to the top of the party and then lost the internal contests that decide who runs it. Candidate-level career panels covering 4,638 candidate-elections in Malaysia’s UMNO (1959–2018), Japan’s LDP (1958–1993), and Taiwan’s KMT (1986–2001) identify which elites exit and when, conditional on a split. Because the party monopolizes access to office, losing an internal contest becomes a choice between marginalization and exit, and defection tracks the internal political calendar. Exits take two forms: bloc exits, when cohesive factions leave together after lost leadership struggles, and marginal exits, when weakened candidates depart alone. Whether a split ends dominance is decided downstream: breakaways endure only when they attach to a social cleavage the parent cannot absorb. Breakdown is an elite phenomenon in its onset and a cleavage phenomenon in its consequences.
“What Race and Ethnicity Hide: Bayesian Approximate Computation with Hierarchical Structure (BACH) for Subgroup Voting Behavior under Partisan Polarization, Cross-Cutting Cleavages, and Survey Nonresponse.” [SSRN] [Poster at PolMeth 2026]
The third paper of my dissertation, “Moving Ground.”
What subgroups of the electorate do is increasingly hidden by the group-level categories our estimators report. BACH couples approximate Bayesian computation with sequential Monte Carlo to infer group-level vote distributions from aggregate election returns: it recovers the full posterior distribution of votes cast by a fine-grained group, such as young college-educated White men, rather than a point estimate with an interval around a one-dimensional average. Even when reporting only race-level results, BACH provides more reliable estimates than classical ecological inference and multilevel regression with poststratification when intra-group heterogeneity is large and survey response is selective, and only BACH’s stated ordering probabilities are well calibrated. The framework is validated on simulations and on the Florida voter file, where national origin rather than education organizes Hispanic vote choice, a within-race cleavage that race-level estimators collapse. An open-source R package accompanies the paper.
“Research Note: A Higher-Order Method of Moments Approach to Ecological Inference under Extreme Survey Nonresponse.” [SSRN]
When surveys are unreliable or absent, as in historical elections and many democracies without polling infrastructure, how can we recover who votes for whom? This research note derives a method-of-moments estimator that exploits higher-order moments of the cross-unit distribution of aggregate election outcomes to identify group voting behavior without individual-level data, offering a closed-form alternative to simulation-based approaches.
“Research Note: Who Counts in 2030? Changes of Representation Under the Proposed Census Exclusions.”
“What the Slope Loses, the Intercepts Gain: Measurement Error and Misattributed Effects in Fixed- and Random-Effects Models” (with Robert Franzese). Under revision.
Fixed- and random-effects models compare each unit to itself over time. When a treatment moves slowly but its measure carries fast-moving error, the within transformation strips out the signal and keeps the noise, and the effect it loses does not simply attenuate; it migrates into the unit intercepts, masquerading as stable “unit characteristics.” Larger samples make this worse, tightening confidence intervals around the wrong value and driving the Hausman test toward the most biased specification. The paper proves the result, establishes a scope condition (unit effects worsen attenuation only when the signal is more persistent than the error), and supplies a diagnose–correct–redesign protocol validated on three datasets.
“Plant Closures and Trump-Related Twitter Discussion: A Spatial-Temporal Description” (with Robert Franzese). Under revision.
How do local economic shocks shape online political extremism? Using a national geocoded tweet corpus matched to plant-closure events across the United States, the paper traces how local plant-closure shocks shaped Trump-related and extremist engagement on social media, mapping the spatial and temporal diffusion of economic-grievance discourse.

The study separates the period, cohort, and life-cycle clocks behind the apparent stability of senior voting blocs.

Hi, I’m Tyler! Welcome to my website.

I am a Ph.D. candidate in Political Science and Scientific Computing at the University of Michigan, where I am also completing an M.A. in Statistics. I am affiliated with the International Institute and the Center for Political Studies. I am also a 2026–2027 graduate fellow at the Michigan Institute for Computational Discovery and Engineering (MICDE).
Substantively, I study how population changes (e.g., urbanization, generational turnover, migration of racial and ethnic groups) and elite politics jointly shape electoral outcomes, political parties and party systems. Methodologically, I focus on ecological inference, hierarchical modeling, simulation approaches, and measurement and inference of Time-Series Cross-Sectional (TSCS) data.
As a MICDE fellow, I notice that the engineering community has a much more cautious yet simultaneously sanguine view about AI. My thoughts on what we mean by AI as Methodology and how to responsibly use AI are published here too.
As a speaker of Mandarin Chinese, Malay, Indonesian, and Japanese, I explore cases across East and Southeast Asia as well as the United States. My fieldwork sites include Malaysia (Kuala Lumpur, Kuala Selangor, Penang, Melaka, Kuala Terengganu, Petaling Jaya, Putrajaya), the United States (Metro Detroit, Metro Milwaukee, and New York City), and Singapore, among others.
My teaching topics include comparative politics, statistical inference and data science, and electoral politics. At UMich, I have co-organized the China Reading Group, a Rackham-sponsored interdisciplinary workshop, since 2023. I also co-organized the Interdisciplinary Workshop on Comparative Politics from 2023 to 2024, and was the president of the Graduate Association of Political Scientists from 2025 to 2026.
My research appears in the Journal of East Asian Studies and in the two leading Chinese-language journals of Southeast Asian studies. My papers, datasets, and CV are linked above.
Outside the academy, I am the dad of two black cats, Erik and Theda, and a volunteer foster with the Humane Society of Huron Valley.

title: Responsible use of AI
text:
I will be publishing my thoughts on how to responsibly use AI as a junior scholar as I navigate the field.


What Do We Mean by AI as a Method?
November 2, 2026






NoteRead essay





Political scientists increasingly talk about AI as a method, and I am not sure I know what we mean by it. Most of my own use of AI is to assist me in coding. But coding is itself a tool, and when AI helps me with coding, it is not offering a new tool so much as taking over a job that I used to do by hand. That alone does not make AI a method. Using a large language model, especially a reasoning model, to analyze text strikes me as a more legitimate case of AI as a method. Beyond that, I am still trying to work out where the boundaries lie.
This may sound like a purely conceptual question, but I think it is a methodological one that we have to address. How we classify a given use of AI determines what we should ask of it. A tool that drafts our code calls for different scrutiny than a model whose judgments become our data. In what follows, I sort the uses I can think of into a few roles. The list is provisional, and part of my reason for writing it down is to find out what I am missing.
The first role is AI as research labor, i.e., AI as a refinement of the research workflow. Here AI writes and debugs code, cleans and merges data, and handles the routine work of building a code base. This is the role I know best, and in my view it does not change our methods at all. A regression estimated with AI-written code is still a regression. What changes is who did the work and who can answer for it. The issues this role raises are therefore issues of data and workflow management: version control, documentation, and whether a human reader can still follow and contest the code. I took up that last problem in my previous essay, “Code as an Artifact in the Age of AI,” where I argued that AI-assisted code must remain readable to human reviewers.
The second role is AI as a measurement instrument, and this is where I think AI becomes a method in the full sense. When a language model classifies legislative speeches by topic, codes protest events from news reports, or places a party manifesto on an ideological scale, its judgments become our data (Stuhler, Ton, and Ollion 2025; Dahlberg et al. 2026; Lowande and Weiss 2026). Text analysis is the clearest example I have so far, though I doubt it will stay the only one. Once AI is an instrument, it should face the standards we apply to any instrument. We need to know whether it measures what we claim it measures, whether it does so consistently, and what exactly the instrument is. That last point is less trivial than it sounds. A commercial model can be updated or retired, which means the instrument that produced our measures may no longer exist by the time someone tries to replicate them.
The third role is AI as a stand-in for human respondents. Some researchers have asked whether a language model, prompted to take on the characteristics of a demographic group, can answer survey questions the way members of that group would, producing what have been called “silicon samples” (Argyle et al. 2023; Kozlowski and Evans 2025; Timoneda 2026). I am the least sure about this role. It is also the most contested, because it depends on whether a model’s answers represent any real population at all, rather than some average of the text it was trained on. If they do, the implications for survey research are large. If they do not, a silicon sample measures the model, not the public. Can we rely on Generative AI to generate data for our research?
These three roles do not exhaust the possibilities, and at least three more belong on the list. First, AI can serve as a treatment. In some experiments, a chatbot is itself the intervention, e.g., when it tries to persuade respondents or deliberates with them (Bai et al. 2025). The methodological question here is what exactly the treatment is, since no two conversations are alike. Second, AI can act as a generator of ideas, helping researchers form hypotheses or synthesize a literature. This role shapes our theory rather than our data, which makes its influence harder to see and harder to report. Third, AI can act as an auditor, checking whether a replication package runs or reviewing another scholar’s analysis. This role connects back to my essay on code, and it carries the same caution: an AI auditor can help a human reviewer, but if AI both writes and reviews the code, no human may ever have understood it.
Laid side by side, these roles suggest an answer to my opening question. Only some of them make AI a method in the strict sense, namely those in which AI produces or shapes our evidence: as an instrument, as a respondent, or as a treatment. The others are uses of AI as labor, as a source of ideas, or as a reviewer. They do not change our methods, but they do change how we account for our work. This is not to suggest that they matter less. If anything, they are more common and less visible, and they raise accountability questions that our field has only begun to take up.
I expect this list to change, and quickly. That is one reason I am writing these reflections here rather than waiting on a journal’s review cycle. Those of us who are early in our careers and use these tools every day are well placed to notice how they are changing our work, even before we have settled language to describe it. If I have missed a role, I would like to hear about it.






Code as an Artifact in the Age of AI
November 2, 2026






NoteRead essay





One of the first things to be automated in the age of generative AI is coding. As methodologists, and as political scientists more generally, we are still working out what we mean by AI as methodology, but I think one of its most fundamental uses is to help us code more efficiently and more accurately. Yet we usually pay attention to whether our code produces the results we want, and rarely think of the code we used to create those results as an artifact that we have to ship.
Replication is not yet an established fact in our field. Although top journals now require replication materials, most journals in political science do not require a fully replicable code base to be deposited in a repository when we publish. What makes things worse is that, because much of our data is sensitive, some code and raw data cannot be deposited even when we want to share them.
In short, I think we neglect code itself as an important artifact, one that demands our attention in the age of generative AI. So the question I keep coming back to is how much attention we should pay to the code. Based on my own work with co-authors, and with generative AI, I have come to believe that replicable research rests, at its foundation, on transparent coding and transparent data sharing. Even when privacy concerns block data sharing, the coding process should at least be transparent.
We now see more and more researchers report that they use generative AI in coding and that they review their results after the code is generated. I would argue, however, that we need to review not only the accuracy of the code but also its readability. Human reviewers should find it easy to read the code and understand what we are trying to do, even when AI assisted us in writing it.
In my understanding, then, a fully responsible use of AI in coding should produce a fully replicable replication package, one that allows any human reader with an adequate understanding of code to reproduce the results by hand and with their own mind, rather than asking another AI to review what the first AI produced. If we write code that produces accurate results but cannot be read by another human coder, the code becomes, in effect, readable only by another AI. That, I think, is a departure from the responsible use of AI. The concern is heightened by an ongoing debate in the software engineering community over whether AI that writes long stretches of code actually understands it. Some argue that these models only predict the next likely piece of code; others see something closer to genuine reasoning in what they produce. That debate is far from settled, and my argument does not depend on how it resolves: whether or not the AI understands the code, a human reader should be able to.
This essay grew out of a recent conversation with a colleague. I felt that I fully understood, and could fully review, the code that AI agents had produced for me, but to him the same code read as too long and too AI-like to follow. The exchange points to a knowledge gap. The researcher who prompts an AI agent to write code knows what they asked for and why, and so has a much better grasp of the code’s structure. A reader who cannot see the prompt has only the code itself, and may find it far harder to work out what each part does and why it is there. Code can therefore be transparent to its author and opaque to everyone else.
I see two potential ways to close this gap. The first is for human researchers to be able to write and revise the code themselves, so that it stays true to how human coders usually understand code, even when AI helped along the way. The second is to keep the AI-generated code but pair it with detailed documentation of the prompts behind it, or to ask the AI agent to record the instructions it worked from while coding, so that readers have the same context the author had. Personally, I think the first is somewhat easier for researchers to do than the second. Yet as the field keeps evolving, and if the trend is to take coding out of human hands entirely, the second may well become the solution.
I am not saying that we should not use AI to assist with coding. What I am saying is that human authors bear the ultimate responsibility for using AI in the right way, and for making sure that our code is actually reviewable and contestable by human readers. That, I think, matters a great deal.
